deadlines.title: RAISE Act
deadlines.scope: Covered frontier-model developers; duties vary by developer size.

deadlines.title: Safe by Design Act
deadlines.scope: Covered social and gaming platforms used by minors, including integrated AI companions.

deadlines.title: SAFE for Kids Act
deadlines.scope: Covered addictive social media feeds and nighttime notifications to minors.

cards.title: Make promises your product can keep
cards.trigger: Start here if you market, demonstrate, or sell an AI product in New York.
cards.rule: GBL §349 now prohibits unfair, deceptive, and abusive business practices. AI accuracy, safety, and performance claims sit within this general business-practices framework.
actions: Check landing pages, demos, sales decks, and onboarding against evidence from the actual version you ship.
Qualify claims such as ‘bias-free,’ ‘100% accurate,’ or ‘replaces a professional’; explain material limitations where the promise is made.
cards.evidence: A dated claims register: the claim, supporting evaluation, limitations, approver, and product version.
cards.boundary: These launch steps apply the general law to AI marketing; New York does not prescribe this particular testing document. The statute’s private remedy for deceptive acts is narrower than the attorney general’s enforcement authority.

cards.title: Know where customer data goes
cards.trigger: Start here if accounts, prompts, uploads, or logs contain New Yorkers’ covered private information.
cards.rule: SHIELD requires reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards. Small businesses receive a proportionate standard, not an exemption. Covered breaches generally require resident notice within 30 days of discovery, subject to statutory exceptions.
actions: Map data sent to model providers and other vendors; document training use, retention, deletion, access, and contractual safeguards.
Assign a security and incident owner. Test access controls, deletion, and the process for assessing a breach and required notices.
cards.evidence: A data-flow inventory, vendor/security terms, retention schedule, and incident-response contacts.
cards.boundary: SHIELD uses a defined category of private information; it is not a universal consent law for all personal data. Other privacy, sector, and children’s-data rules may also apply.

cards.title: Build cancellation before billing
cards.trigger: You sell consumer subscriptions, automatic renewals, or trials that turn into paid plans.
cards.rule: GBL §527-a requires clear renewal terms, affirmative consent, a retainable acknowledgment, and simple cancellation through the same medium used to subscribe. Specific trial, renewal, and change notices also apply.
actions: Show price, billing interval, renewal, and cancellation terms before consent. Let users keep their acknowledgment.
Test signup-to-cancellation on mobile and desktop. Add the reminders required for your trial length, renewal period, or planned price change.
cards.evidence: Screenshots of checkout and cancellation, consent records, and scheduled-notice templates.
cards.boundary: This provision concerns consumer purchases for personal, family, or household purposes. Do not assume every enterprise SaaS contract has the same rules.

cards.title: Disclose personal-data pricing at the price
cards.trigger: An algorithm uses an individual consumer’s personal data to set their price.
cards.rule: GBL §349-a requires the conspicuous disclosure: ‘THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA.’ A general privacy-policy statement is not a substitute for the required pricing disclosure.
actions: Identify which inputs actually set prices, including behavioral profiles and inferred willingness to pay.
Place and test the required notice with affected prices across checkout, experiments, and mobile views.
cards.evidence: Pricing-input documentation and screenshots of the notice beside each affected price.
cards.boundary: Personalized pricing and ordinary price changes are different scope questions. Assess statutory definitions and exemptions; this entry does not address separate rent-setting rules.

cards.title: Classify the relationship your chatbot creates
cards.trigger: Your AI is designed to sustain a human-like relationship, remembers interactions, and engages personally with users.
cards.rule: Covered companions need reasonable-efforts self-harm response protocols and crisis referrals, plus non-human identity notices at the start of an interaction and every three hours of continued use. The initial notice need not repeat more than once daily.
actions: Document whether memory, emotional prompts, and ongoing conversations put the product within the companion definition.
Test crisis-response paths and recurring notices across long sessions, reconnects, and mobile use; assign a human owner for incidents.
cards.evidence: A scope assessment, notice schedule, crisis-response test cases, and incident process.
cards.boundary: Specified customer-service, technical-assistance, research, and internal-productivity uses are excluded. A chatbot is not automatically a companion. For minors on covered platforms, also plan for Safe by Design.

cards.title: Treat teenagers’ data as a launch requirement
cards.trigger: You know a New York user is under 18, or your online service is primarily directed to minors.
cards.rule: The Child Data Protection Act has applied since 20 June 2025. Nonessential processing of 13–17-year-olds’ data needs informed consent; under-13 processing follows the law’s COPPA standard. Consent must be separate from the transaction. Covered minors’ data cannot be sold.
actions: Separate processing necessary to provide the requested service from advertising, optional analytics, and model-training uses; assess each purpose.
Build age-aware choices and withdrawal flows. Check processor agreements and honor applicable age signals.
cards.evidence: A purpose-by-purpose data map, age-signal handling, consent screens, and processor terms.
cards.boundary: An adult cookie banner or a consent sentence buried in general terms is not a reliable substitute. The statutory necessary-processing exceptions must be assessed individually.

cards.title: Put the January 2027 youth rules on your roadmap
cards.trigger: You run a covered social or gaming platform, integrate an AI companion, or offer a covered personalized social feed to minors.
cards.rule: Safe by Design takes effect 1 January 2027: covered platforms face age-assurance and minor-default protections, including integrated companions disabled by default for minors unless a parent overrides. SAFE for Kids follows on 25 January 2027 for covered addictive feeds and nighttime notifications.
actions: Assess each law separately against the platform’s actual features and audience; plan age assurance, parent controls, and restricted defaults before release.
For covered social feeds, design the required parental-consent path and nighttime-notification controls. Test behavior when consent is absent or withdrawn.
cards.evidence: Separate scope decisions for each act, a dated engineering plan, and default/consent-flow test results.
cards.boundary: These are two different laws. Safe by Design has a specific platform definition; SAFE for Kids does not cover every AI recommendation. A standalone chatbot is not automatically a covered social or gaming platform.

cards.title: Agree who owns the hiring-tool audit
cards.trigger: You use or sell AI that substantially assists or replaces decisions in hiring or promotion connected to NYC.
cards.rule: For covered AEDTs, NYC Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit within the preceding year, a public summary, and applicable 10-business-day notices. Employers and employment agencies carry these duties. State and city discrimination protections remain relevant.
actions: Check the tool definition and job location, including remote roles associated with an NYC office.
If you supply the tool, prepare audit-support data and documentation; agree responsibilities with the customer. If you hire, verify the audit, publication, and notices before use.
cards.evidence: A scope assessment, auditor relationship, dated audit/publication record, notices, and customer responsibility matrix.
cards.boundary: Buying a vendor’s ‘compliant AI’ label does not transfer the employer’s duties. Passing the prescribed audit is not a discrimination safe harbor.

cards.title: Separate AI labels from likeness permissions
cards.trigger: Your ads use a synthetic person, or your product uses someone’s face, likeness, or voice for advertising or trade.
cards.rule: GBL §396-b requires disclosure for covered synthetic performers in ads. Civil Rights Law §51 separately permits claims over unauthorized use of a real person’s protected identity in advertising or trade. Covered fashion work adds specific digital-replica consent duties.
actions: Decide whether an asset depicts an invented performer, an identifiable real person, or both; assess the relevant rule for each use.
Secure required written permissions and keep them tied to the asset, purpose, and version. Add the synthetic-performer disclosure where required.
cards.evidence: An asset and release register, approved usage terms, and final ad screenshots.
cards.boundary: The synthetic-performer definition has exclusions, including certain audio and expressive-work uses. Adding an AI label does not itself provide permission to clone a real person.

cards.title: Prepare for a regulated buyer’s due diligence
cards.trigger: You sell AI software to a DFS-regulated financial institution or insurer.
cards.rule: DFS guidance directs regulated firms to assess third-party cyber risks, including AI use and customer-data training. Insurance guidance addresses AI underwriting/pricing governance and discrimination. Buyers may need contractual access to supplier information and controls.
actions: Prepare answers on data provenance, model limitations, security, subcontractors, retention, and whether customer data trains models.
Discuss testing evidence, change notification, incident support, audit/regulator cooperation, and data return or deletion before the procurement review.
cards.evidence: A reusable buyer packet: model documentation, evaluation results, security summary, data-processing terms, and change/incident contacts.
cards.boundary: These sources address regulated firms. Selling software to a bank does not automatically make the startup a Part 500 covered entity; buyer contracts can still impose obligations. Direct financial services need a separate scope review.

cards.title: Check your developer role before applying RAISE
cards.trigger: You train or initiate training of a foundation model at the statutory frontier-compute threshold.
cards.rule: From 1 January 2027, RAISE imposes tiered duties on covered frontier developers. The definition uses more than 10²⁶ training operations; the large-developer tier uses annual gross revenue above $500 million, including affiliates.
actions: Record who trains the model and the relevant compute, including material modifications, then assess New York scope and developer tier.
If covered, map transparency and incident reporting before deployment; large developers must also plan their safety framework and additional duties.
cards.evidence: A role/compute assessment, release documentation, and reporting ownership where the act applies.
cards.boundary: An app built on someone else’s API is not automatically a frontier developer. Being below the large-developer revenue threshold does not remove all duties if you meet the frontier-developer definition.

cards.title: Design for the NYC customer’s physical setting
cards.trigger: Your product identifies customers with biometrics or controls access to NYC residential buildings.
cards.rule: NYC’s customer-biometric law adds notice and monetization restrictions for covered establishments. Its tenant-data law separately regulates covered smart-access systems. State security duties can apply alongside these local requirements.
actions: Ask where the system will be installed and whose data it captures: retail customers and residential tenants trigger different reviews.
Build configurable collection, retention, deletion, and access controls; agree with the customer who handles required notices and tenant processes.
cards.evidence: An installation-specific data map, retention settings, notice plan, and customer/vendor responsibility record.
cards.boundary: These are activity-specific NYC additions, not a statewide blanket ban on facial recognition. Assess the operator, building or establishment, and statutory exceptions.
